one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban follows up his foundational Grace Poe citizenship column with a Q&A on reader reactions. The most exhilarating: an early email from UNHCR's Bernard Kerblat calling CJP's opinion 'a pleasant soothing philharmonic orchestra composition to our ears,' providing badly needed clarification that a foundling in the Philippines is not stateless -- contrary to some uninformed voices -- and declaring 'YES, the UNHCR FULLY supports' CJP's call for PH accession to the 1961 Convention on the Reduction of Statelessness. On June 16, Kerblat, deputy Yasser Saad, and legal aide Iya Gallardo visited CJP at home; they explained that during a December 7, 2011 ministerial meeting, the Philippine panel pledged to initiate accession to the 1961 Convention, and that in February 2015 various executive agencies convened to develop a national plan to end statelessness by 2016. Paulino Yusi, a Makati lawyer, objected that Article 2's presumption of Filipino parents does not ipso facto make Poe natural-born -- under the 1935 Constitution, Filipino-mother/foreign-father children need to elect Philippine citizenship upon reaching majority. CJP answers: the 1961 Convention refers to 'parents,' so it is enough that her presumed father is Filipino; Poe derives natural-born citizenship from her presumed Filipino father and need not elect, because her presumed father already conferred that status at birth. Joselito Basilio from Dubai argued Article 2 is based on jus soli while our Constitution is based on jus sanguinis -- incompatible. CJP answers: there is no incompatibility; the 1961 Convention simply says a foundling is presumed to have parents who are nationals of the country where found, and under PH Constitution citizenship follows the father or mother. Ray Lopez from California praised CJP for explaining the issue 'devoid of bias' and criticized critics as 'intellectual prostitutes.' CJP clarifies he met Poe only once at a public forum and has had no other official or personal association. The tougher question, posed by multi-awarded journalist Marites Vitug and Eric Damasing: while Poe may have acquired natural-born citizenship via generally-accepted-principles, she lost it when she married her American husband -- and by taking an oath of allegiance to reacquire it, did she perform 'an act to acquire or perfect her Philippine citizenship,' thereby losing natural-born status? CJP answers no, citing David v. Agbay (March 18, 2015): under RA 9225, natural-born citizens who became citizens of another country before the law's effectivity reacquire Philippine citizenship upon taking the oath, while those who became foreign citizens after the law's effectivity retain their citizenship upon taking the same oath. Since Poe belongs to the first category -- a reacquirer, not a retainer -- she reacquired her original natural-born citizenship. Her taking the oath of allegiance is not 'an act to acquire or perfect'; she had already acquired and perfected her citizenship at birth. Ineluctably, she reacquired the same original natural-born status.
